docs.title: Fast DDD
docs.text:
Domain-Driven Design for FastAPI services.

fast-ddd gives you Aggregate, Entity, and ValueObject building blocks, wired together with Repository and UnitOfWork abstractions, so you can start from a tested structure instead of assembling one from scratch.

Your domain model stays independent of the database: business rules live in plain Python objects and can be tested without a database.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• Domain building blocks: Aggregate, Entity, ValueObject.
  • Persistence-ignorant domain: the domain model knows nothing about tables or sessions.
  • Repository and Unit of Work: a clear way to load, save, and commit changes.
  • FastAPI integration: dependency-injection-friendly, so it fits normal FastAPI code.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Supports python version 3.13 and later.

pip install fast-ddd

docs.title: A minimal example
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from fast_ddd import Aggregate, ValueObject, Uow

class Money(ValueObject):
    amount: int
    currency: str

class Order(Aggregate):

    def pay(self) -> None:
        # business rules and invariants live here, not in the API layer
        ...

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PayOrderPayload:
    order_id: int

class PayOrderCommand:
    def __init__(self, uow: Uow):
        self._uow = uow

    async def execute(self, payload: PayOrderPayload):
        async with self._uow:
            order = await self._uow.orders.get_by_id(payload.order_id)
            order.pay()

        # auto-committed

The application service loads an aggregate through a repository, calls domain behavior on it, and commits through the unit of work. It never touches the database directly.

docs.title: Is this for you?
docs.text:
fast-ddd targets services, including small microservices, whose business logic is complex enough that the domain model should not be tied to the database schema.

If your service is mostly CRUD, an Active Record framework such as Django (with its admin) is probably the better choice. See Motivation for the full reasoning and the trade-offs.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
This repository makes Domain-Driven-Design (DDD) practical for FastAPI services.

It provides domain utilities such as Aggregate, Entity, ValueObject and wires them together with Repository and UnitOfWork abstractions, so new projects can start from a tested structure instead of assembling one from scratch.

docs.title: Why not just use Active Record (Django, Tortoise ORM)?
docs.text:
Django's ORM and Tortoise ORM follow the Active Record pattern: a model class corresponds to a table row and carries its own persistence behavior ("the object saves itself").

In Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, Martin Fowler notes that this works well when domain logic is simple, and that it becomes awkward as logic grows more complex (Fowler, 2002).

The reason is coupling. With Active Record the schema and the domain model are the same thing, so:

  • business rules are shaped by table structure instead of by the domain;
  • schema changes ripple into domain code, and vice versa;
  • rich domain concepts (value objects, polymorphism, invariants spanning several objects) have to be squeezed into one-class-per-table;
  • domain logic is hard to test without a database.

For domains with complex business rules, Fowler recommends a Domain Model combined with Data Mapper, which keeps the domain objects and the database independent of each other.

In DDD this means you first model the domain from business rules, and then design the database schema separately to suit storage and query needs (Evans, 2003). Repository and Unit of Work then give the domain a persistence-ignorant way to load, save and commit changes (Percival and Gregory, 2020).

If your service is mostly CRUD, Active Record (and Django with its admin) is a sound choice. This project targets the other case: services, including small microservices, whose business logic is complex enough that the domain model should not be tied to the database schema.

docs.title: "But we don't do much upfront domain modeling"
docs.text:
You don't need a big upfront design phase to benefit from this approach. Whether or not you plan it, you will model the domain in code: every business rule you implement, every name you choose and every constraint you enforce is part of a domain model. The only question is whether that model is explicit or accidental.

The same problems then surface later, just more expensively:

  • the same rule is implemented in several places and they drift apart;
  • invariants hold on some code paths (the API) but not others (admin, bulk updates, scripts);
  • it is unclear which objects must change together, so transaction boundaries and consistency rules become accidental;
  • renaming or splitting a domain concept forces a schema migration, so refactoring the model means refactoring the database;
  • business rules can't be tested without a database;
  • logic drifts out of the objects into services, leaving an anemic domain model, where objects are little more than data holders (Fowler, 2003).

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
This approach is not free. Separating the domain model from persistence buys independence and testability, and you pay for it.

  • More code and more layers. You write the domain classes, the persistence models (or tables) and the mapping between them. A simple "add a field" change may touch several places.
  • Learning curve. Teams need to understand aggregates, repositories, unit of work and persistence ignorance. Misapplied, DDD vocabulary produces ceremony without benefit.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Make the benefits of DDD accessible not only to large applications but also to microservices with complex business logic.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software (Addison-Wesley, 2003), ISBN 0321125215. Evans introduces model-driven design, in which the code is the model.
  • Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (Addison-Wesley, 2002), ISBN 0321127420, Chapter 10.
  • Martin Fowler, "Anemic Domain Model," martinfowler.com bliki, 25 November 2003, https://martinfowler.com/bliki/AnemicDomainModel.html
  • Harry Percival and Bob Gregory, Architecture Patterns with Python (O'Reilly, 2020), ISBN 9781492052197. Covers the Repository and Unit of Work patterns, with persistence-ignorant domain code, in Python.
